subtitle: Saying one thing and doing another, and playing with words
words.intro: No German host has ever said *Please go home now*. There’s a code: *Es ist schon spät*. *Morgen muss ich früh raus*. Someone brings the coats. At C2, you can read this code. Below that, you stay until you’re sent home with the leftovers.

grammar[0].fact: A *Litotes* denies the opposite. *Nicht unklug* isn’t the same as *klug*: it’s cooler, and it keeps some distance. Northern Germans may go a lifetime without any stronger praise. *Kann man essen*, about your best dish, is a compliment in Hamburg.

grammar[1].fact: German headlines love a pun, and a broadsheet may run one above a very serious story. *Steuer* is the classic: one is what you pay, and the other is what you hold when you drive. There’s a whole genre of bad jokes built on it, and you’re now cleared to tell them.

document.intro: This is another kind of reading between the lines. It’s a real leaflet from a Nazi district leader, in the last months of the war. He says there’s no reason to worry. Read what he says about the rumours. Then ask yourself why anyone would need to print this.
document.fact: Soon afterwards the Red Army reached Meseritz, and the German population fled or was driven out. It’s now Międzyrzecz, in Poland. A person who could read this properly knew exactly what to do, and the last sentence told them what it would cost.

reading.intro: Lena and Max have had friends to dinner. It’s ten to one. All the guests have gone but one: Herr Kolb, the retired examiner. He has just been brought another glass of water, and he’s telling them about the 1987 driving test regulations. Max and Lena have tried everything.
reading.fact: German directness is famous, but it’s a myth about half the time. At the door, it’s another thing: Germans are known for the long goodbye, the *Abschied im Flur*, in which the most important talk of the evening starts with one arm in a coat. Count on twenty minutes.
